name: Saint Margaret Parish Church — Lehel Square
description: The Árpád-házi Szent Margit-templom, popularly the Lehel tér church, is a neo-Romanesque parish church in Újlipótváros designed by István Möller and modelled on the Zsámbék church ruin. Built from 1931 to 1933, it has frescoes by Henrik Heintz and stained glass by Miksa Róth.

children.text: The Árpád-házi Szent Margit-templom, the Church of Saint Margaret of the House of Árpád, is popularly known as the Lehel téri templom, the Lehel Square church. It is a Roman Catholic parish church in Budapest's thirteenth district. Hungarian Wikipedia gives its address as Váci út 34, 1132 Budapest, in the Újlipótváros neighbourhood, and says it stands on Szent Margit tér, a small square separated from Lehel tér on 29 May 2019.

The parish grew out of a Chapel Association founded in 1919. A parish community formed in 1920 under Gyula Zaymus, and in 1923 it became an independent parish. The church was built between 1931 and 1933 to plans by István Möller, who based them on the ruins of the church at Zsámbék; the master builder was Ferenc Wihart. It was consecrated on 15 October 1933 by Cardinal-Primate Jusztinián Serédi. The total cost was about one million pengő, which the community paid off through donations.

The style is neo-Romanesque, and Hungarian Wikipedia links the thick walls, square towers and portal to the medieval atmosphere of the Zsámbék model. The interior has frescoes by Henrik Heintz, statues by György Nemes Ősz, and stained glass and a rose window by Miksa Róth. A planned altarpiece by Ferenc Chiovini, St Stephen's Missionary Journey, was never completed.

The church took the name Árpád-házi Szent Margit in 1944, after the canonisation of Margaret; before that it was dedicated to Blessed Margaret. It suffered minor damage in the Second World War and was repaired with donations. In 1975 a new liturgical space was designed by Gyula Bárdos, and from 1988 to 1994 the roof, stained glass and interior painting were renovated.

The church sits at the edge of a busy junction. Hungarian Wikipedia describes the neighbouring Lehel Csarnok market hall, built in 2002 to a design by László Rajk Jr. and nicknamed the Kofahajó, on the site of the old Lehel market. The article on Lehel tér lists the M3 metro, which has a Lehel tér station.
Good to know
This is a working parish church. Check with the parish for current Mass times and when visitors can enter.
Maps may show the church under either Lehel tér or Szent Margit tér, and the street address is Váci út 34.
Look at the rose window and stained glass by Miksa Róth, and the frescoes by Henrik Heintz.
The Lehel Csarnok market hall next to the church is a short walk away.

historyIntro: The Lehel tér church was built in 1931 to 1933 by a parish that had begun as a chapel association in 1919. It was designed by István Möller in a neo-Romanesque style modelled on the Zsámbék church ruin.

children.text: Hungarian Wikipedia records that the Chapel Association was founded in 1919 and that a parish community, Lipótváros II, was formed in 1920 under Gyula Zaymus. In 1923 it became an independent parish, and part of Terézváros was attached to it.

István Möller designed the church, basing his plans on the ruins of the church at Zsámbék, and the master builder Ferenc Wihart carried out the work. Construction took place between 1931 and 1933, and Cardinal-Primate Jusztinián Serédi consecrated the church on 15 October 1933. The floor area is 918 square metres. The total cost was about one million pengő, which the community paid off through donations. The interior frescoes are by Henrik Heintz, the statues by György Nemes Ősz, and the stained glass and rose window by Miksa Róth.

historySections.heading: A new name, war damage and renovation

children.text: The church took the name Árpád-házi Szent Margit in 1944, after the canonisation of Margaret; it had previously been called Árpád-házi Boldog Margit. In the Second World War it suffered minor damage, which was repaired with donations from believers. In 1975 a new liturgical space was designed by Gyula Bárdos, and between 1988 and 1994 the roof, stained glass, interior painting and electrical wiring were renovated. On 29 May 2019 Szent Margit tér was separated from Lehel tér, and the church now stands on that square.

name: Saint Ladislaus Church — Kőbánya
description: Ödön Lechner's Kőbánya church mixes Romanesque, Gothic, Renaissance, Baroque, Persian and Hungarian folk motifs. Built from 1894 to 1899 and consecrated in 1900, it has Zsolnay tiles and altars, and among Budapest churches only St Stephen's Basilica is taller than its 83-metre tower.

children.text: The Kőbánya Saint Ladislaus Church, in Hungarian the Kőbányai Szent László-templom, stands at Szent László tér 25 in Budapest's tenth district. It is a Roman Catholic parish church, owned by the Kőbánya local government according to Hungarian Wikipedia. The Budapest City Archives describe it as a church by Ödön Lechner, built on the site of a former rowing lake. Lechner's father owned a brick factory on Maglódi Street, and the archive notes that Lechner lived in Kőbánya at the time.

The commission was complicated. According to the City Archives, Lechner received the commission in 1891, and his first design, in an unusual Byzantine style with Eastern ornament, had to be revised at the client's request. A second version was also rejected. A third, eclectic and Secessionist, was approved, but Lechner was removed from the project when he judged the deadline unachievable; about a hundred artists then petitioned that the interior should be by the same architect as the exterior. Hungarian Wikipedia counts the designs differently and says Lechner prepared the final design in September 1893.

Construction ran from 1894 to 1899. The cross was blessed on 12 August 1897, and the faithful took possession of the church on 2 April 1899. It was consecrated in June 1900; Hungarian Wikipedia's text gives 27 June, St Ladislaus's day, while its infobox says 28 June. Lechner's style combines Romanesque, Gothic, Renaissance, Baroque, Persian and Hungarian folk elements. The tower is 83 metres high, and in Budapest only St Stephen's Basilica is taller.

Look for the colourful Zsolnay roof tiles outside and the Zsolnay majolica altars and pulpit inside. One side altar was donated by the brewer Antal Dreher, and the stained glass and mosaics are attributed to the workshop of Miksa Róth. The Second World War damaged the building badly, with the original stained glass destroyed, and the Hussar tower burned in 1957.

A long restoration followed. Hungarian Wikipedia dates the complete renovation to 1974 to 1994, while a We Love Budapest article says major reconstruction began in the 1980s and ended in 2001, so sources differ. A statue of Saint Ladislaus by Károly Antal stands in front of the church.
Good to know
This is an active parish. Check the parish website, szentlaszlo.net, for Mass times and visiting arrangements before you go.
Kőbánya is away from the central tourist area, so plan your route and travel time in advance with the city's public transport planner.
Look up at the roof tiles and the tower; the Zsolnay ceramics are the church's most distinctive features.
Read the Budapest City Archives article on the church's design history, which explains why Lechner's plans changed.

historyIntro: The Kőbánya church was designed by Ödön Lechner after a difficult commission and built between 1894 and 1899. It was consecrated in 1900 and is today owned by the Kőbánya local government.

children.text: According to the Budapest City Archives, Ödön Lechner received the commission for a parish church in 1891, on the site of a former rowing lake. His first design, in an unusual Byzantine style with Eastern ornament, had to be revised at the client's request, and the second version was also rejected even though it followed the requested pointed-arch form. The third, eclectic and Secessionist, was approved, but Lechner was removed from the project because he judged the deadline unachievable. Hungarian Wikipedia gives a different account: it says Elek Barcza was first commissioned, that Lechner took over, and that his final, fifth design dates from September 1893.

Construction ran from 1894 to 1899, with Lechner as site supervisor and János Szabó as contractor according to Hungarian Wikipedia. The cross was blessed on 12 August 1897, and the faithful took possession of the church on 2 April 1899. About a hundred artists petitioned the council that the interior should be designed by the same architect as the exterior; the interior works went to Ottó Tandor, who designed the altars, pulpit and baptismal font. The church was consecrated in June 1900; the article's text gives 27 June, the feast of Saint Ladislaus, while its infobox gives 28 June.

The building suffered serious damage in the siege of Budapest in the Second World War. Visitor information from We Love Budapest says the Zsolnay roof and towers were damaged and that stained glass by Miksa Róth was destroyed and later recreated by Tibor Bráda from the original plans. In 1957 the Hussar tower burned down. Hungarian Wikipedia says a complete renovation began in 1974 and ended in 1994, and that the church regained protected monument status in 1991; We Love Budapest says major reconstruction began in the 1980s and finished in 2001. A proposal to rename Kőbánya Szentlászlóváros, made around the time northern Transylvania returned to Hungary, was never carried out.

stories.title: Lechner's changing designs

children.text: The Budapest City Archives describe how Lechner's proposals were revised more than once. His first design was Byzantine in character, the second was rejected although it was pointed-arch in form, and a third, eclectic and Secessionist design was approved. The archive states that Lechner was then removed from the project over the deadline, and that about a hundred artists petitioned for the interior to be designed by the same architect as the exterior.
Hungarian Wikipedia counts the designs differently, so sources do not agree on the exact sequence.

name: Óbuda Synagogue
description: The Óbuda Synagogue at Lajos utca 163 is a neoclassical synagogue consecrated in 1821 and designed by András Landherr. After decades as a warehouse and television studio it was rededicated in 2010 and is again an active Orthodox prayer house maintained by EMIH, a Chabad-linked community.

children.text: The Óbuda Synagogue, in Hungarian the Óbudai zsinagóga, stands at Lajos utca 163 in Óbuda, Budapest's third district. Its website calls it the capital's oldest functioning Jewish prayer house, and says it is maintained by the EMIH, the Unified Hungarian Israelite Community. The congregation is Orthodox, and Hungarian Wikipedia says Chief Rabbi Slomó Köves has led it since 2010. It is a living place of worship with a weekly schedule of prayer and study.

Jews resettled in Óbuda in the early 18th century under the protection of the Zichy family. The synagogue's history page says that by 1727 they could hold public worship, and that in 1738 construction began on the first synagogue. A Baroque synagogue by Máté Nöpauer followed in 1767 to 1769, but its walls cracked because of poor foundations and unstable soil. In 1817 the Buda Building Committee chose to rebuild it while keeping most of the walls.

The present building is the result. Hungarian Wikipedia credits András Landherr with the design, work began around 1820, and the synagogue was consecrated on 20 July 1821. It received a new south façade with a columned porch of six Corinthian columns and a tympanum inscribed with a Hebrew verse from 1 Kings. The main hall has 662 fixed seats, 364 for men and 298 for women, and a wooden Torah reading table in the centre surrounded by four Empire-style obelisks.

The 20th century was hard on the building. About 3,000 Óbuda Jews died in the Holocaust, according to Hungarian Wikipedia, and from the 1960s the building was sold and used in turn as a museum, a warehouse and a television studio; Magyar Televízió used it as Studio 5 from 1978. In spring 2010 EMIH took it over, and it was rededicated on 5 September 2010. Restoration work included repainting about 25,000 small Stars of David on the vaults, and the restored synagogue was formally reopened on 12 April 2016.
Good to know
This is an active synagogue and prayer house. Check obudaizsinagoga.hu for current visiting arrangements, services and events before you go.
Respect the prayer schedule: the site lists daily services and a Shabbat programme, so visits should be arranged around them.
Across the street, at the corner of Lajos utca and Zichy utca, a We Love Budapest article places the oldest house in the third district, now an exhibition space of Budapest Galéria.
Pair the visit with a walk around Óbuda; English Wikipedia says that when the synagogue was built, Óbuda's was the largest Jewish community in Hungary.

historyIntro: The Óbuda Synagogue was consecrated in 1821 as a rebuilding of an earlier Baroque synagogue. From the 1960s it was sold and used as a museum, warehouse and television studio, and it was rededicated for worship in 2010.

historySections.heading: A Jewish community under Zichy protection

children.text: Jews settled in Óbuda in the early 18th century, mainly from Moravia; a 1712 census lists 24 families, or 88 people. They lived under the protection of the Zichy family, and by 1727, according to the synagogue's history page, they could hold public worship, acquire property and run their own courts in exchange for a protection payment. By 1737 the community had 43 families, and in 1738 construction began on the first synagogue, which Countess Zichy ordered enlarged in 1746. A Baroque synagogue by Máté Nöpauer followed in 1767 to 1769, but its walls cracked because of poor foundations and unstable soil.

In 1817 the Buda Building Committee assessed the cracked synagogue and chose to rebuild it while keeping most of the walls. Architect András Landherr began work around 1820. The building received a new south façade, a columned porch and a new roof, and was consecrated on 20 July 1821. The main hall has 662 fixed seats, 364 for men and 298 for women. In 1900 the synagogue was renovated by architect Gyula Ullmann with Art Nouveau elements, and electric lighting was installed.

historySections.heading: Deportation, a studio and the return of worship

children.text: Hungarian Wikipedia records about 3,600 members in 1944, down from 5,500 in 1929, and says around 3,000 Óbuda Jews died in the Holocaust. After repairs in 1946 and 1947, the Jewish school was closed by the state in 1948, the Óbuda congregation merged into the Budapest congregation in 1949, and the building was listed as a protected monument in 1957. From the 1960s the building was sold and used as a museum, a warehouse and, from 1978, a Magyar Televízió studio. In spring 2010 EMIH took over the building, which was rededicated on 5 September 2010 and reopened for worship on 8 September. The restored synagogue was formally reopened on 12 April 2016.
Hungarian Wikipedia records that in the great flood of 1838 the water reached the Ark in the Óbuda Synagogue, and that members of the community rowed in to rescue the Torah scrolls.
